title: Μέλισσαι καὶ Ζεύς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 234. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Μέλισσαι φθονήσασαι ἀνθρώποις τοῦ ἰδίου μέλιτος ἧκον πρὸς τὸν Δία καὶ τούτου ἐδέοντο ὅπως αὐταῖς ἰσχὺν παράσχηται παιούσαις τοῖς κέντροις τοὺς προσιόντας τοῖς κηρίοις ἀναιρεῖν.
sentences.tr: Melissai phthonēsasai anthrōpois tou idiou melitos hēkon pros ton Dia kai toutou edeonto hopōs autais ischyn paraschētai paiousais tois kentrois tous prosiontas tois kēriois anairein.
sentences.l: Bees, having grudged men their own honey, came to Zeus and begged of him that he furnish them strength to destroy, striking with their stings, those who approach the combs.
sentences.i: The bees, grudging men the honey they counted as their own, came to Zeus and begged him to give them the strength to strike with their stings and kill anyone who came at the combs.
sentences.n: φθονέω takes the dative of the person grudged and the genitive of the thing, so ἀνθρώποις … τοῦ ἰδίου μέλιτος is 'grudged men the honey that was their own'. ἴδιος carries the whole complaint: the bees think of the honey as theirs and of men as thieves. ὅπως with the subjunctive after a verb of asking gives the content of the request; παιούσαις is a dative participle agreeing with αὐταῖς.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Ζεὺς ἀγανακτήσας κατ’ αὐτῶν διὰ τὴν βασκανίαν παρεσκεύασεν αὐτάς, ἡνίκα ἂν τύπτωσί τινα, τὸ κέντρον ἀποβαλεῖν, μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο καὶ τῆς σωτηρίας στερίσκεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Kai ho Zeus aganaktēsas kat’ autōn dia tēn baskanian pareskeuasen autas, hēnika an typtōsi tina, to kentron apobalein, meta de touto kai tēs sōtērias steriskesthai.
sentences.l: And Zeus, having grown angry at them over their malice, arranged for them, whenever they strike anyone, to cast off their sting, and after this to be deprived of their preservation as well.
sentences.i: And Zeus, angered at them for their malice, so arranged it that whenever they struck anyone they should lose the sting, and after that their life as well.
sentences.n: βασκανία is malice of the envious sort — the word behind the evil eye — and the moral picks it up again in βασκάνους. σωτηρία is preservation, staying alive; being deprived of it is dying.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος ἁρμόσειεν ἂν πρὸς ἄνδρας βασκάνους οἳ καὶ αὐτοὶ βλάπτεσθαι ὑπομένουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos harmoseien an pros andras baskanous hoi kai autoi blaptesthai hypomenousin.
sentences.l: This story would fit spiteful men, who even submit to being harmed themselves.
sentences.n: ὑπομένω is to stand one's ground and take what comes; the spiteful accept their own hurt as the price of the other man's.
